Force and Laws of Motion

Force

  • Force is an external agent capable of changing a body's state of rest or motion. The SI unit of force is Newton (N). A newton is defined as 1 kg m/s².
  • The Force has different effects, and here are some of them:
  • Force can make a body that is at rest to move.
  • It can stop a moving body or slow it down.
  • It can accelerate the speed of a moving body.
  • It can also change the direction of a moving body along with its shape and size.

Force produces the change in velocity.

Balanced and Unbalanced Force

#### Balanced Force

  • Balanced forces are forces that cancel each other out because they are equal in strength and act in opposite directions. The net force acting on an object when forces are balanced is zero (F_Net = 0).

#### Unbalanced Force

  • Unbalanced forces are forces that are not equal in magnitude and/or act in the same direction. The net force acting on an object when forces are unbalanced is not zero (F_Net ≠ 0).

#### Illustrations

  • Balanced Force: When the man pushes against the wall, the forces at play balance each other, and as a result, the wall does not move.
  • Unbalanced Force: One person significantly heavier than the other creates a condition of unbalanced forces in a seesaw.

#### Case 1 vs Case 2

  • Case 1: 10 N ↔ 10 N → Balanced Force, Net Force = 0, Acceleration = 0
  • Case 2: 20 N → 30 N → Net Force = 10 N, Unbalanced Force

Types of Force

  1. 1. Contact Forces: A contact force is a force that acts on a body either directly or through a medium are called contact forces.
  • Frictional Force: Frictional Force refers to the force generated by two surfaces that contact and slide against each other.
  • Spring Force: The spring force is a restoring force exerted by a spring when it is stretched or compressed.

Hooke's Law: It states that the force needed to extend or compress a spring (or any elastic material) by a certain distance is directly proportional to that distance.

  1. 2. Non-Contact Forces: A non-contact force is a force applied to an object by another body that is not in direct contact with it.
  • Gravitational Force: A gravitational force is an attractive force between two masses.
  • Magnetic Force: Magnetic force is the force experienced by a moving electric charge/magnetic material in a magnetic field. It can also refer to the attractive or repulsive interaction between magnetic materials or magnets.
  • Electrostatic Force: The electrostatic force, also known as the Coulomb force, is the attractive or repulsive force between two electrically charged objects.

TRICK to Remember non-contact forces: GEM (Gravitational, Electrostatic, Magnetic)

Conservative ForcesNon-Conservative Forces
Work done is independent of the path (depends on final and initial point)Work done depends upon the path
Work done is zero in case of a closed pathWork done is not zero in case of a closed path
Work done by it is completely recoverableWork done is not completely recoverable; some energy is lost (usually as heat)
E.g. Gravitational force, electrostatic, magnetic, spring forceE.g. Frictional force, Drag

Friction drag is a force that resists the motion of an object moving through a fluid (air/liquid).

Order of Force: Static Friction > Sliding Friction > Rolling Friction

Laws of Motion

  • Galileo Galilei first proposed the concept of inertia. By observing the motion of objects on an inclined plane Galileo deduced that objects move with a constant speed when no force acts on them.
  • Galileo published a series of essays named: De Motu (Meaning: "On Motion")
  • Galileo's first book: La Bilancetta ("The Little Balance") published in 1586.
  • Newton formulated the three laws of motion.

Force and Laws of Motion (continued)

1st Law of Motion → Law of Inertia

  • The Law of Inertia states that "An object at rest remains at rest and an object in motion remains in motion at constant velocity unless acted upon by an external force".

#### Types of Inertia

  1. 1. Inertia of Rest: This is the tendency of an object to remain at rest unless acted upon by an external force. E.g. The dry leaves and fruits falls when we shake a tree.
  2. 2. Inertia of Motion: This is the tendency of an object to continue moving in a straight line at a constant speed unless acted upon by an external force. E.g. A person sitting in a moving car may be pushed forward when the car stops abruptly as our legs are in contact with the surface.
  3. 3. Inertia of Direction: This is the tendency of an object to continue moving in the same direction unless acted upon by an external force. E.g. When a car makes a sharp turn, your body tends to move in the direction it was previously moving, rather than following the car's new direction.

Inertia: The tendency of an object to resist changes in its state of motion. It depends on the mass of the object.

Inertia ∝ Mass

2nd Law of Motion

  • The 2nd Law of Motion states that force equals mass times acceleration, or F = ma. This law describes how the acceleration of an object depends on the force applied to it and the object's mass. E.g. A cricketer pulling back his hand while catching the ball to avoid injury.

Force = Rate of change of momentum

F = ma

F = Kg m/s²

Derivation:

Change in momentum = mV − mu

Rate of change in momentum with time = (mV − mu) / t

We know (V − u)/t = a (acceleration); = m(V − u)/t = ma

3rd Law of Motion

  • The 3rd Law of Motion states that "For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction" meaning if one object exerts a force on another, the second object will exert an equal and opposite force back on the first. E.g. When a gun fires, the bullet experiences a forward force, and the gun experiences an equal and opposite force, causing it to recoil backward.

Questionnaire

A constant force acts on an object of mass 5 kg for a duration of 2s. It increases the object's velocity from 3 m/s to 7 m/s. Find the magnitude of the applied force. Now if the force were applied for a duration of 5 s. What would be the final velocity of object?

Sol:

F = m × a

F = m × (V − u) / t

F = 5 × (7 − 3) / 2

F = 5 × 4/2 = 10 N

10 = 5 × (V − 3) / 5

10 = V − 3

V = 13 m/s

Impulse and Momentum

  • Momentum measures the "quantity of motion" of an object, defined as the product of its mass and velocity. The S.I. unit of Momentum is Kg m/s.

p = m × v

  • p = vector quantity
  • m = scalar quantity
  • v = vector quantity
  • Impulse is the change in momentum of an object caused by a force acting over a short period of time.

Impulse-Momentum Theorem: F Δt = m ΔV

Conservation of Momentum

  • The conservation of momentum principle states that "In a closed system, the total momentum remains constant", meaning momentum is neither created nor destroyed, but only transferred.

Force and Laws of Motion (continued)

Conservation of Momentum (continued)

  • In the equation, m₁ and m₂ are masses of the bodies, u₁ and u₂ are the initial velocities of the body and v₁ and v₂ are the final velocities of the bodies (change in velocity not mass).

Conservation of momentum equation: m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂

Questionnaire

A girl of mass 40 kg jumps with a horizontal velocity of 5 m/s onto a stationary cart with frictionless wheels. The mass of the cart is 3 kg. What is her velocity as the cart starts moving?

Sol:

  • Mass of girl (m₁) = 40 kg
  • Velocity of girl before jump (u₁) = 5 m/s
  • Mass of cart (m₂) = 3 kg
  • Velocity of cart before jump (u₂) = 0 m/s
  • Final velocity of girl + cart system = v

m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂

(In this case, v₁ = v₂ = v)

40 × 5 + 3 × 0 = (40 + 3) × v

200 = 43v

v = 4.65 m/s
